job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I walk to work in Vienna, to a six-person startup that builds ordering software for restaurants. I'm the junior developer, so I build small features, fix bugs and answer questions from customers when something breaks at dinner time. I studied software engineering at the technical university, and I did one internship at an insurance company.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the founders let me try things, and that a feature I built can be in use the same week. What wears me out is the uncertainty of a young company. I rent a small flat with my cousin Sofie, and my parents run a bakery in Graz, which I help with when I visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and a lot of noise around it. At work I'd keep using it, and at home I'd tell my parents it's a calculator for words. A bakery and a software firm both live or die on whether customers come back, and no tool changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. I use AI all day to write code faster, and our small company would rather have one person who uses it than two who don't. I have no debt, seven months of savings and a family that would back me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: build the features the founders ask for, learn how our customers actually run a kitchen, and save 500 euros a month. I'd keep helping at the bakery on visits and think about what software it needs. I'd go to church with my mother when I'm in Graz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored by the hype. I'd rather be building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools every day. What do you use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant writes a draft, I run it, break it, and write the tests. It also helps me read old code that nobody documented. I'd say it saves me about two hours a day, and I'm still the one who decides what ships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of the bakery's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents think the bakery will always have customers, and that's probably true. But ordering, pricing and waste are a mess, and software could help. I'd love to build them something, and I might do it as a side project.

feel: **Calm**, and a little bored by the hype.

steps.text: Build the features the founders ask for and visit customer kitchens
Sketch ordering software for my parents' bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news if you work, and a challenge if you don't. At work I'd suggest we use it more in customer support and testing. A business that uses these tools well can do with six people what used to take twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm and a bit excited. In a small company the people who can use the tools are the ones who get more responsibility, and I'd likely get more. The risk is that the founders decide they need only two developers, and I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on customer-facing tasks and learn how to run our systems. I'd ask the founders for a share of the company's growth, like some options. I'd put 700 euros a month into savings and a bit into shares, and use my weekends to build the bakery's ordering tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with a pinch of nerves. I think the market rewards the people who move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks would the machine take next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Support answers and basic tests, probably this year. I already use it to draft answers for customers, and I'd say it handles about half. I'd still read every one before it goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your startup still hire juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, but fewer. The founders say they'd rather hire one experienced person than three juniors. So if I leave, I might not be replaced. That is how it works, and I don't like it, but I understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shift and I'd want to be honest about it. At work I'd say the company should plan for what happens when the tools can do my job. If a machine can write my code for free, I need to own something, because wages won't be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious, to be honest. Writing software is the first thing on the list, and in two years a restaurant software firm might need one person and a lot of computers. Robots for hands-on work are three years behind, which helps the bakery more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 1,200 euros a month, and start my own small firm selling the ordering tool to bakeries and cafés. I'd go after ten customers in the first year. I'd also move into my parents' flat above the bakery for a while if I needed to, because that would take rent off the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a lot of drive. I'd feel I had to act quickly, and that's better than freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to fifteen bakeries and cafés and ask what they'd pay for. I'd leave my job only when I have three paying customers. It's risky, but I'm comfortable with risk, and my savings would give me a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep making bread, because ovens and hands are three more years' work at least. And I'd say that I want to be useful to them, with an ordering and pricing system. My father would say that I'm a good girl and a bit crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window, and I'd tell friends to start something. At work I'd learn every part of the business. Five years is long enough to build a company, and short enough that you can't wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy rather than scared. By 2031 a lot of coding will be done by machines, but companies still need people who know customers and take responsibility. I think a small firm that builds on top of the machines could do well, and I'd want to be one of the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd build the ordering tool with the bakery as my first customer. By year two I'd have a handful of customers and keep my job part-time. I'd save 800 euros a month and put some into an index fund. If the firm works in year three, I'd go full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and a bit nervous. I'm in a good position and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now, but carefully, in the evenings, so I keep my wage. The robots' delay gives hands-on firms like bakeries a few more years, and they need help with the thinking side. That's my market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the firm now or later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also volunteer to help the church's community kitchen with ordering. It's a small thing, but it keeps me in touch with real customers, and it's good to give something back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build something solid, and I'd tell everyone to learn and save. At work I'd keep growing. Ten years is long enough to build a business, a home and a family, and still be ready for a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pretty calm. At 32 I could have my own firm or a good senior role, and people who use these tools well should be fine. I'd worry about people who don't have a family bakery or savings behind them, and I'd want to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job a couple of years and start my business on the side. I'd save for a flat in Graz, near my parents, and take a part-time course in business. I'd use every new AI tool as soon as it works, and I'd teach my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade feels like a long runway, and I like to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if you knew it was ten years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to marry around 27 or 28, and have children by 30. I'd like to live near my parents, and keep going to church. The date doesn't change that. If anything, it makes me want to settle sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about family and home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd sprint and hope. With ten I'd build carefully and take fewer risks. It's the same person, but I'd be kinder to myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I like risk and I use these tools daily, but two years is short even for someone who likes to move first. What would help is clear information from companies, cheap business loans for small firms and training that people can take at night.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm lucky to have a family business to lean on. I'd like policies that reward work and help people start something, rather than just paying them to wait.

headlineQuote: I like risk and I use these tools daily, but two years is short even for someone who likes to move first.
portrait: Yara is **22**, a software engineering graduate working as a junior developer at a six-person Vienna restaurant-software startup.
She uses AI tools daily, has no debt and seven months saved, and her parents run a bakery in Graz.
She is traditional and pro-market, **blames** red tape more than firms, and values work, family and church.
She is adaptive: she acts early, plans a **small firm** of her own and times her leap with customers.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because two years is short even for someone who moves first.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **information** from companies, cheap business loans for small firms and evening training.
